title: Blade Runner, Gnosticism, and the more than human
subtitle: A soul in a machine
author: Gigla Gonashvili
introduction: What does it mean to be human — and could a machine become one too? For philosopher *Gigla Gonashvili,Ridley Scott’s Blade Runner is not a film about artificial intelligence but something older and stranger: fallen angels, trapped light, and the secret of human nature. Here, Gonashvili argues that humanity is defined not by the film's famous empathy test, but by a sense of shared mortality, and an elegiac awareness that every captured moment is already slipping away.
body:
The world of Blade Runner (1982) is a graceless world. Unlike its sequel, which appeared thirty-five years later, the original film does not entertain the idea of a messiah, a miracle, a child born of synthetic humans. It is dark, gritty, in a film noir sense, in which the villain outshines the supposed hero. As the bounty hunter (called “blade runner” in the film), Deckard rather unwillingly accepts his assignment—to retire, that is, to kill—the humanoid robots called replicants, he gets immersed in a world which seems to make him doubt how he should act (and this goes, perhaps, for Harrison Ford as well, who plays the hunter). After all, the name Deckard sounds rather close to Descartes—the philosopher for whom radical doubt was a method, and the body foremost a machine.

Enter Roy Batty (Rutger Hauer), with his demonic glow and his quest for a life that is, if not immortal, at least properly long—and worthy of the name. In the film’s final moments, Deckard finds himself hanging from a rooftop in pouring rain. He is spared. Batty delivers a now iconic monologue—“Tears in Rain”—which Hauer rewrote the night before the scene was shot, stripping the original script down to pure poetry. A replicant, a machine, prepares to relinquish his synthetic soul; and yet he wonders at all the glorious moments he has lived and seen. He speaks from within an intimate paradox: “all those moments will be lost in time, like tears in rain.” There, he voices a deeply human truth—of a creature who, while not a machine, is still a material, composed being, susceptible to degradation and to the ultimate dissolution. After all, the word “human” carries an elegiac hue: homo, from humus, means the earth, the clay, the ground to which we return.

Fallen angels

The world of the original Blade Runner is also that of a Fall. “Fiery the angels fell,“ Roy Batty recites, misquoting William Blake (who wrote, in America: A Prophecy, “fiery the angels rose“). The inversion is not accidental. These beings, created for free labor in off-world colonies, rebel against their original purpose and original design, and descend to the underworld—which is Earth in this case: Los Angeles in 2019, a city submerged under pollution and near-incessant rain, marked by its pyramid-like buildings and industrial fires.

Thus, they disobey their original purpose and depart in search of a maker who cannot—or will not—give them what they need. Dr. Eldon Tyrell resides at the very top of a pyramidal Tyrell Corporation. Roy and the others find their way to his chamber: only to hear, from Tyrell, that their meagre four-year lifespans cannot be extended. Roy, disappointed and enraged, kills him, crushing his skull by pressing his thumbs into his eyes and squashing them.

SUGGESTED VIEWING Overcoming death With Patricia MacCormack, Anders Sandberg, Janne Teller, Rowan Pelling

The film toys with Gnostic themes. Tyrell is a god of the underworld, an arrogant—short-sighted, or rather blind—Demiurge, who traps the divine spark (the synthetic soul, composed of implanted memories) into inert, imperfect matter. The Gnostic world is, after all, that of strict oppositions: the spiritual world (Pleroma) and the inherently flawed material world (Kenoma).

In this sense, the film seems to pay homage to the author of the book from which it was adapted, Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? Not only was Philip K. Dick deeply immersed in Gnostic mysteries—see, for instance, his Exegesis, a work of many sleepless nights running to thousands of pages—but his strict distinction between humans, who possess empathy, and machines, which do not, implies the evil side of matter. This dualism is given its most concrete form in the Voigt-Kampff test: a procedure designed to locate empathy as the criterion of humanity, premised on the assumption that the line between human and non-human is sharp, measurable, and real.

And yet the film, famously, goes further. The replicants—Nexus-6 models, the most advanced ever created—are supposed to be more human than human, as the Tyrell Corporation’s slogan has it. “We’re not computers, Sebastian, we’re physical,“ says Roy, and his companion Pris follows with “I think, Sebastian. Therefore I am.“ This rather unexpected emphasis on the physical implies that the replicants have feelings, a sense of purpose, or at the very least an experience of “accelerated decrepitude“—Pris’s word—which they share with humans.

It has been noted that the replicants of Blade Runner are rather the fallen angels of Paradise Lost. Not only does Satan (Lucifer) rebel—“Better to reign in Hell, than serve in Heav’n“—and outshine God himself (an “ill-tempered, sanctimonious bore,“ as Harold Bloom put it), emerging as the more charismatic figure; but the world of Paradise Lost, despite all its cosmic battles (inspired in part by the ongoing civil wars in Milton’s England), remains a monistic world, in which the angels are sensuous beings—not only the fallen ones, but the unfallen too: “the angel with a smile that glowed / Celestial rosy red, love’s proper hue“ (VIII, 618–19). It is a fascinating historical detail that Paradise Lost was completely dictated, as Milton had already lost his eyesight. Despite his blindness, it seems he managed to keep both the fallen and unfallen worlds united within the exact same vision.

The eye, photographs, and the nostalgia of a lost world

Eyes are everywhere in Blade Runner. Not only does the film open with an extreme close-up of a human eye—vast, unblinking, in which the infernal skyline of Los Angeles is reflected—but there are constant allusions to its perfect design, to the moments captured and held by these eyes.

“Chew, if only you could see what I’ve seen with your eyes,“ Roy Batty tells Hannibal Chew, the craftsman who, as he himself says, “only do[es] eyes.“ And in the famous monologue we are told what exactly those eyes have seen: attack ships on fire off the shoulder of Orion; C-beams glittering in the dark near the Tannhäuser Gate.

Eyes carry something more. Ridley Scott and cinematographer Jordan Cronenweth used a special technique: a half-mirror mounted in front of the lens to reflect light directly into the actors’ irises, producing an unnatural gleam suggestive of replicant nature. In certain scenes, this technique was applied to Deckard as well—a clue alluding to the possibility that the blade runner himself might be a replicant.

In Blade Runner, humans and replicants are drawn together—not only by their shared susceptibility to physical decrepitude, but by the irretrievable loss that attends the passing of time.

Eyes are there to capture something more—an interiority, a sense of lived time. They are, in this sense, rather like cameras. After all, doesn’t Rachael—a replicant who does not know it—carry photographs that remind her of a supposed past (with her mother), which are in fact implanted memories, moments that are not hers? When confronted with this possibility (rather brutally, by Deckard), she breaks down in tears, feeling robbed of her past and her identity. Deckard, unable to bear it, tells her it was just a joke—a bad joke.

With this motif of unreal photographs, the film introduces the theme of nostalgia, of something lost, or rather touched with a forlorn temporality, simply because it has been captured. Susan Sontag wrote:

Photography is an elegiac art, a twilight art. Most subjects photographed are, just by virtue of being photographed, touched with pathos. An ugly or grotesque subject may be moving because it has been dignified by the attention of the photographer. A beautiful subject can be the object of rueful feelings, because it has aged or decayed or no longer exists. All photographs are memento mori. To take a photograph is to participate in another person’s (or thing’s) mortality, vulnerability, mutability. Precisely by slicing out this moment and freezing it, all photographs testify to time’s relentless melt. (On Photography, 1977)

Yet a photograph evokes more than a hopeless flight from time. As Roland Barthes puts it:

In front of the lens, I am at the same time: the one I think I am, the one I want others to think I am, the one the photographer thinks I am, and the one he makes use of to exhibit his art. In other words, a strange action: I do not stop imitating myself, and because of this, each time I am (or let myself be) photographed, I invariably suffer from a sensation of inauthenticity [...] I am neither subject nor object but a subject who feels he is becoming an object: I then experience a micro-version of death [...]: I am truly becoming a specter. (Camera Lucida, 1980)

What we have here is a falling apart—or more aptly, an interior distancing and alienation—which imbues the moment of capture with a sense of loss. The world of Blade Runner is that of vast distances, exemplified also by the music of Vangelis: music full of echoes and resonances, enveloping experience within some immaterial realm, no longer present but still haunting. Identity, memories, captures of lived moments—these float freely in this realm, unsure what to do with themselves. Touched by absence (or rather, absences, in the plural), they can no longer embody the vast armature of time; they can only escape from it and long for some impossible return. Hence their nostalgia.

A world before us

We live, now, in an age of total inscription. Everything is photographed, recorded, stored, uploaded, archived. We have become extraordinarily good at preserving our moments; and, perhaps, progressively less certain that those preserved moments are truly ours. Not because we might be replicants, but simply because this outlasting of data makes our place in time uncertain. Does it even matter that we have lived through all those moments? There is no immortality for us. Only mementos—foreshadowing the imminent death. As if we were to say, in allusion to Roy’s monologue: all those moments will be lost—and therefore preserved—like orphaned data drifting through the cloud.

Proust wrote, in the final volume of his monumental work—Time Regained—that the true paradises are the paradises we have lost. He meant that moments stored as particularly significant memories erupt in medias res without the promise of restoring an old order. They make us breathe, he wrote, a new air, precisely because it is air we have already breathed: the air of freshness, of beginning, already constituted as such in memory. They are moments of singularity: always beginning, always departing, always commencing anew—even in a world which seems doomed to its fate. In the very last lines of Paradise Lost, as Adam and Eve receive from the archangel Michael the whole prophecy of mankind—including the birth and crucifixion of the Messiah—the poem closes thus: “The world was all before them, where to choose / Their place of rest, and Providence their guide: / They hand in hand with wandering steps and slow, / Through Eden took their solitary way.“

SUGGESTED VIEWING I forget therefore I am With Oliver Hardt, Iain McGilchrist, Catherine Loveday, Jessica Frazier

In Blade Runner, humans and replicants are drawn together—not only by their shared susceptibility to physical decrepitude, but by the irretrievable loss that attends the passing of time, and equally by the preservation of moments inscribed deep within their (synthetic) souls. They are bound by a strange nostalgia, by the strange imprint of a gaze that always touches us from a distance. And they are united, too, by the enigma of more human than human.

It is as if it were always our purpose—to surpass our humanity, to become creators, to establish our own reign on earth, in nature, in society—but it seems that humans themselves may have become submerged by this more, by the deluge of artifacts and data. When the horizon is thus closed, there is no other side; there is no “more.“ It is perhaps here that an actor steps in and inhabits a role already written, yet open enough to allow something more—an elegiac monologue, tears in rain. As Rutger Hauer himself put it: “Half of Roy belongs to me, or half of me belongs to Roy.“ It is a strange confession—and a telling one. This union, this exchange of souls, this substitution marks our imagination—which is human, and perhaps more than human.
